newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia politician warns of return to savage past.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia politician warns of return to savage past.

text.p: Cambodian's powerful parliament chief on Wednesday appealed to the main political parties to end an escalating feud over the monarchy or risk a return to the country's bloody past.

But as Chea Sim called for calm, hardline Khmer Rouge guerrillas took sides in the deepening rift in Cambodia's governing coalition, pledging allegiance to a political alliance led by First Premier Prince Norodom Ranariddh.

"I appeal to all politicians and all political parties to resolve together the problems of our nation with the sense of responsibility," Chea Sim said in his speech, urging the government to "protect our policy of national reconciliation."

He warned that divisions in the coalition government could bring "the return of the country to the terrible past that existed before the Paris Peace Agreements," which ended decades of war in 1991 and paved the way for democratic elections.
More than one million Cambodians lost their lives in the brutal 1975-78 rule of the ultra-leftist Khmer Rouge.

Chea Sim also praised the stabilising role of King Norodom Sihanouk, whose talk last month of abdication sparked the latest crisis between the Cambodian People's Party (CPP) and the royalist FUNCIPEC party.
The two rival parties have lurched from one dispute after another after, forming a tense coalition government following U.N.-run polls in 1993.

But the CPP on Wednesday said it backed a statement last weekend by Second Prime Minister Hun Sen that he would ask Sihanouk to ban royal family members from politics unless they renounced their royal status and warned he would cancel coming elections if the king abdicated to enter politics.
The popular Sihanouk has said that while he is unhappy on the throne, he has no plans to run for office.
Local and national polls will be held this year and in 1998.

Speaking on hardline Khmer Rouge radio on Wednesday, nominal guerrilla leader Khieu Samphan said he backed Ranariddh and an alliance the prince formed recently with other political parties and "strongly opposed Hun Sen's communist party."
The Khmer Rouge reneged on the Paris peace accords and have been fighting the coalition government.
Decimated by defections, the less than 2,000 hardliners are now thought to be negotiating for peace with the government.
